# isQuitWindowAllClo callback relationships

Originally, all that remained on this page was a name that was easy to read too much into: `isQuitWindowAllClo`. When it was circled in `ElectronNET.Host/api/app.js`, the note beside it said "quit after all windows are closed?"; the question mark stayed. That line was not a conclusion about the interface, but a starting point left over from reviewing the old host script.

The old notes broke the name down very literally: `Quit` suggested quitting, `Window` suggested windows, and `AllClo` was casually read as "all closed." That breakdown helped locate the code, but it also led to an old assumption: the window-close action and the quit check should be in the same callback chain. The first draft placed the two next to each other on that basis, as if the quit check already had a result as soon as the close action occurred.

This version keeps that assumption because people reviewing the old code often start right here, but it can no longer be treated as a confirmed relationship. A name may appear near window handling, or it may be passed to another local entry point. Without seeing where it is passed, "all closed" and "quit" are just two terms guiding where to look, not the two ends of a control-flow path.

## First-draft margin notes

The few lines in the original notes did not preserve the full context, leaving only this sequence:

```text
ElectronNET.Host/api/app.js
        │
        ├─ isQuitWindowAllClo
        │
        ├─ window close-related locations
        │
        └─ event / failure exits
```

This is not a runtime flowchart. It is only the order of paging through the same file at the time: first landing near the name, then looking at the local section containing the window-close code, and finally going back to find where control flow exited. The diagram shows no arrow directions because the first draft did not copy down the section of code needed to establish the direction.

Putting event and failure side by side back then did not mean the two kinds of exit were equivalent, either. An event exit is where a piece of processing passes information out of its current location; a failure exit may only represent a branch that did not complete. The old notes left no specific names for these two locations, so we cannot attribute arbitrary error handling to `isQuitWindowAllClo`, or claim, conversely, that all window events pass through it.

## Interpretations revised after review

The review first withdrew the interpretation "the name looks like a predicate, so it must determine whether the windows are closed." The available notes include neither parameters nor a return value, and do not mark it as a public interface. Calling it a callback in this page's title and the old annotations only describes a relationship with the surrounding processing that still needs investigation; that is not enough to infer that it returns a Boolean, accepts a window object, or directly makes the decision to quit the host.

The second change was to remove "the last window" from the notes' default assumptions. The first draft said "after all windows are closed," but neither the filename nor the name itself preserved any evidence for "the last one." Keeping the pointer to the window-close area is enough. If a later reading turns up special branches for multiple windows or a single window, update the notes to reflect those actual branches; do not override them with this old page's shorthand.

The third change was to stop treating adjacent code in the file as callers. The direct dependencies, window-related handling, and failure branches that appear in `app.js` may just be neighbors in the same script. The first draft did not make that distinction, so it looked more certain than the underlying material supported.

When starting at `isQuitWindowAllClo`, first find where it is declared, stored, or passed on in the file. If what you see is a variable handoff, stop the notes at that handoff; do not infer an event registration from the name. Then go back to the handling near window closing and check whether it actually leads to the same name. If the two locations cannot be connected, keep them as parallel leads.

If an event path can be traced here, also examine separately how it leaves the current snippet. An event being handed on elsewhere is a different reading from a failure branch exiting early. The old draft grouped them together as "exits" just to avoid overlooking the edges of the file; that does not mean they converge, or that either has been confirmed to belong to this callback.

The first draft's "may check whether to quit after all windows are closed" has not been deleted. # Bridge 12 Requirements History

## Starting with an old script that did not fit

The first note from 5 2023 did not start at the lifecycle entry point for Electron.NET. The team first had an old investigation trail to follow: both the issue name and the call name matched `ElectronNET.WebApp/wwwroot/assets/highlight.min.js`. The search terms included `host`, `window`, `reuse`, `mode`, `main`, `app`, and `url`, so the file was marked as pending verification for Bridge 12 readiness.

That page recorded three names side by side: Reuse the watch-mode main window, Preserve BrowserWindow progress options, Route authenticated BrowserView proxies. Recording them side by side was only a way to avoid omitting any of the requirement names used at the time, not an indication that they already shared a common call chain. The first version had no window creation code, no options diff, and no call snippet for proxy requests.

The judgment at the time was straightforward: first, continue looking through the matched file. That judgment was not later discarded wholesale, because it did explain where this history began; what needed to be retained was only "start searching here", not "the window behavior is implemented here".

## The filename once carried too much meaning

The old records treated `highlight.min.js` as a file near the entry point. The repository index described its local role as an existing js module for code reading and verification of historical behavior. This description was much narrower than "window compatibility layer".

The location that can be rechecked in the current revision is `ElectronNET.WebApp/wwwroot/assets/highlight.min.js:3`. The text in that section begins with `var t=...`, followed by `r={keyword:...}` and a series of syntax-category entries. Here, `var t` is a matching-rule declaration, and `r` is a structure resembling a keyword list. This can explain why the old search matched those terms, but it cannot show that the file contains `createBrowserWindow`, a BrowserWindow lifecycle, or authenticated BrowserView proxies.

The path was therefore not removed, but the interpretation was narrowed. The navigation record still points to `internal/ENB`'s `v_prev`, but that record preserves only the relationship between the file and the revision. The file's directory, the matched terms, and runtime responsibilities are no longer automatically equated.

## 2024 addendum: Names return to their respective objects

The review first separated out the window reuse item. It involves the relationships among watch mode, main window, requested URL, and duplicate window. What needs to be checked is the window-creation entry point, the existing main-window object, and where the URL comparison occurs in the creation flow. The regular expression declarations in the highlighting module alone cannot establish the order of these actions.

The second item is BrowserWindow progress options. The concern here is whether existing options continue to be passed through the compatibility bridge when a window is first created. That is a different question from whether an existing window is reused. There are no constructor arguments or option-passing snippets, so this page cannot turn the name into a statement that they "have been preserved".

The third item is authenticated BrowserView proxies. This requires seeing the actual BrowserView, the selected session, and which layer forwards authentication details and proxy parameters. The old record retains only the topic name, with no proxy code for this page to cite. Nor can it be assigned to the highlighting module merely because `host` or `route` appears.

The limited decision after the review was to keep the three topics in the same readiness history, while retaining a separate verification target for each topic. They remain adjacent in the directory, but their technical classifications are no longer merged.

## An on-the-spot search that yielded no results

One focused review searched for `url`,`equals`,`once`,`instead`,`duplicate` on the same line. The combination of terms suggested that "there might be one-time window handling when URL values are equal", and also made duplicate window a counterexample worth watching for. But that search provided no call stack, no information on changes to window instances, and no user-side results.

The only thing that could be recorded at the time was therefore a working hypothesis: watch mode might need to handle existing windows conditionally. The review did not record "possible" as a pass, nor did it record the number of reload operations as a confirmed fact. Its result was to distinguish between two kinds of evidence: term matches can determine where to look next, but only direct code evidence can establish window behavior.

This distinction also affected the other two items. No conclusion was reached on progress options merely because `window` appeared on the same line; session ownership was not established for authenticated BrowserView proxies merely because `host` appeared. That search produced no commands, test numbers, or new call entry points, so the status remained unresolved.

## The original plan remains here

> First search the text of `highlight.min.js`, then use `window` and `reuse` to locate the window behavior; if the terms are adjacent, add compatibility logic here.

This was an early working judgment, preserved unchanged on this page. It was later overturned by the content on line 3, because the matched content belonged to a syntax-highlighting module, not confirmed window lifecycle code. The path still has value for searches, but the earlier inference about the implementation is no longer used.

Another earlier version put the three readiness names on the same row of a to-do table, followed only by "confirm the calls". This is not being deleted either. It shows that the issues were treated as a group to close out at the time, but it did not prove that the three topics shared an owner, an entry point, or a scope of changes. The three names can still be used to look back at the history, but that combined judgment cannot be carried forward.

Keeping the old paragraphs is important: if only the current account were retained, readers would not see why a syntax-highlighting file was once included in the investigation path for the window issue; if only the path were retained, readers would mistakenly assume that the path was the implementation location. Both kinds of records are retained, and the old plan is marked locally as outdated.

## Boundaries established by the review

A sentence that recurs in the review records is:`The actual relationship is still determined by the references in that revision`. It has not been changed into a stronger guarantee. There are only two points in scope here: paths must be reviewed alongside `internal/ENB`,`v_prev`; file locations must not be presented as proof of runtime responsibilities.

The review left three separate tracks. The first examines the `createBrowserWindow`,`app.mainWindow` and URL checks in watch mode. The second only checks BrowserWindow construction or the passing of progress options. The third checks the actual forwarding of BrowserView, the authentication context and proxy parameters. The three tracks share the readiness directory but do not share a conjectured block of code.

The review did not recast "not found" as "does not exist". It only required the record to remain at the file-navigation level when the material still stopped at line 3. This keeps the distance between paths, local declarations and the missing direct object visible.

## Old example: An error in a follow-up check

An early follow-up check treated adjacent search hits for `window` and `reuse` as an entry point for window reuse and was preparing to continue searching for `duplicate`. This example is outdated but still illustrates how the error arose: search terms point to text and do not automatically point to objects.

Another old example was putting BrowserWindow progress options and authenticated BrowserView proxies in the same to-do paragraph. That seemed concise for scheduling but would actually bring issues with the BrowserView session into the window-options checks. This page retains that adjacent wording but no longer treats it as a functional boundary.

## The current decision is in the second half

By the most recent review, the window-creation relationship in watch mode already had a precise description that could be cited independently:

`In watch mode, createBrowserWindow reuses app.mainWindow when the requested URL equals mainWindowURL and calls reload exactly once instead of constructing a duplicate window.`

This sentence appears only once on this page. It limits the object to `createBrowserWindow`, the existing window to `app.mainWindow`, and the comparison target to `mainWindowURL`, while also defining the relationship between reload and duplicate window. It does not extend to BrowserWindow progress options being retained, nor to authenticated BrowserView proxies having completed routing.

Therefore, the scope closed out by this decision record is local. watch mode must preserve the above relationship: retain the existing main window, keep URL equal, and call reload only once; the other two remain adjacent readiness topics, awaiting their respective direct material. When there is no window-options transfer snippet, do not write a result for progress options; when there is no BrowserView/session proxy snippet, do not write the completion status of authenticated proxies.

This conclusion also corrects the earlier way of merging them. The three names can continue to appear on the same page because together they formed the Bridge 12 readiness record at that time; only one window behavior is currently established, and it cannot be used to close out the other two topics.

## One preserved relationship diagram

```mermaid
stateDiagram-v2
    [*] --> SearchAnchor
    SearchAnchor: old issue name and call name
    SearchAnchor --> LocalDeclaration
    LocalDeclaration: highlight.min.js line 3
    LocalDeclaration --> UnconfirmedObject
    UnconfirmedObject: window options and proxy calls
    UnconfirmedObject --> WindowBehavior
    WindowBehavior: watch mode's main-window relationship
    UnconfirmedObject --> OptionCheck
    OptionCheck: BrowserWindow progress options
    UnconfirmedObject --> ProxyCheck
    ProxyCheck: BrowserView authenticated proxies
```

The diagram does not connect the local declaration directly to the window implementation. It preserves the path that actually appeared in this history: the earlier investigation first reached the file; line 3 narrowed the file's responsibility, and only afterward did it split window behavior, window options, and authenticated proxies into three verification directions.

## Remaining downstream adjacent issues

`highlight.min.js` still helps explain why the earlier investigation matched these words. It cannot answer three object-specific questions: whether the actual implementation entry point for `createBrowserWindow` is in the same file as that script; whether progress options are passed individually when BrowserWindow is created; which session stores and forwards the authentication context for authenticated BrowserView proxies.

The status of these three items is different from "this feature does not exist". This page has no frozen material establishing success, failure, or ownership, so only the questions themselves are retained. In particular, `r={keyword:...}` on line 3 must not be treated as a runtime exception, nor can an old path be treated as evidence of a missing implementation.

This adjacency record also constrains where subsequent supporting material belongs. If new material is window construction code, it can initially change only the evidence for the window topic; if the material concerns passing BrowserWindow options, it belongs under the progress options topic; only if the material is a proxy snippet involving BrowserView and session is there reason to change the authenticated proxy status. The same highlighted statement cannot be used to substitute one of the three for another.

## Meeting and Review Excerpts

The early meeting notes grouped the three readiness names together to look for user paths that were not yet covered. A later review split them into three areas: window creation, window options, and authenticated proxies. The former explains the grouping, and the latter explains why that grouping cannot imply a shared implementation.

Another comment from the discussion retained in the review was: `The actual relationships are still determined by the references in that revision`. On this page, it serves only to verify paths and was not written as a commitment to completion. Thus, `ElectronNET.WebApp/wwwroot/assets/highlight.min.js`, `internal/ENB`, and `v_prev` remain a set of historical navigation information, not an inventory of runtime components.

This review also recorded a practical trade-off: the page would retain the three readiness names, but only the window topic, which already had precise object relationships, would be closed out. If the two items without direct supporting material were deleted, the history would lose the reason for continuing the investigation at the time; if they were all marked complete, the page would go beyond what the existing records can support.

## Old Appendix

### Example 1: Making Changes Based on Adjacent Words

The old example took the textual adjacency of `window`, `reuse`, and `duplicate` to indicate the window entry point. The syntax-matching declaration on line 3 later exposed the problem with this inference. The example is retained as a record of a misreading and cannot be used to determine where to make changes.

### Example 2: Three Names Share One Line

The old to-do item once read: Reuse the watch-mode main window, Preserve BrowserWindow progress options, Route authenticated BrowserView proxies——verify the call. It was not deleted, because that was how the first version recorded it. Now only name-based searches are carried forward, not the assumption that "one call can cover all three items".

### Example Three: Partial Source Code Excerpt

```text
ElectronNET.WebApp/wwwroot/assets/highlight.min.js:3
var t=... ,r={keyword:...}
```

This excerpt only supports returning to the old file to inspect the declarations. It is retained alongside `internal/ENB`,`v_prev`, and the regexes and keyword table cannot be used to infer the window lifecycle, progress options or BrowserView authenticated proxies.

### Example Four: Names and Objects Were Not Aligned

Early records treated "main window" as an adequate verification target, but did not also record the creation method, the URL comparison value or the window instance field. Later supplementary notes separated these terms, and only then did it become clear that "there is a main window" and "a particular request will reuse that window" are not the same judgment. This example adds no new runtime conclusions, and only preserves the change in how things were recorded.

### Example Five: Treating Directory Relationships as Implementation Relationships

All three topics fall under Bridge 12 readiness, so the old example interpreted directory adjacency as code adjacency. The current page still retains the historical traces left by this arrangement, but discusses directories and objects separately.`highlight.min.js` can serve as a navigation entry point, but being listed in the same set of materials does not give it the responsibilities of BrowserWindow or BrowserView.

## Where the Evolution Leaves Us

This page ultimately retains three different kinds of material: one watch mode window behavior proven suitable for standalone citation; one judgment about a file that has already been refuted by part of the source code, but still has search value; two readiness topics that the materials on this page have not yet resolved. The current position is presented after the old paths, rechecks, search attempts, review excerpts and old examples, so readers can still see how the judgments narrowed.

If direct objects are added back later, they should map to window construction, the BrowserWindow option, or the BrowserView/session proxy, respectively. Adding back only the same highlighting module declaration is not enough to change the status of the other two items. The page can continue to reference ENB-201, ENB-209, and ENB-228 as navigation for these three topics, but these cards do not replace the local decisions already retained on this page.

- For async open and IPC, find one entry point still in use for each, preserve caller expectations first, and do not assume a common return convention.

# Bridge 12 Interface Trial Plan

This proposal originally brought three topics into a single review: image writes, completion timing for opening externally, and the arguments for BrowserView IPC. This arrangement was only meant to keep the scope of the Bridge 12 discussion manageable, not to imply that they share a call chain. When cited, the old page has often been read as "change all three together." We retain that starting point here, along with the reasons the topics were later split apart.

The initial assessment of image handling was unreliable. At the time, seeing `import { clipboard } from 'electron';` at the top of `ElectronNET.Host/api/clipboard.ts` led to the provisional assumption that the serialized representation could be passed directly to the write operation. That explains why the investigation started from the host API, but it does not establish what object the Electron side accepts. Based on that assumption, the first draft recommended starting with a combined trial; that recommendation did not result in a single combined change.

The follow-up review split the issues into three distinct gates. For images, the first question is where the representation becomes an image that can be written; for Shell.OpenExternal, whether the caller really needs a completion signal; for BrowserView, what argument sequence the existing route receives. Asking these questions first is not a way to postpone the issues, but a way to avoid applying a conclusion from one entry point to the other two.

## Retained Earlier Plan

The old plan was to cover all three with one bridge change, then use one round of integration testing to decide whether to proceed or revert. It had two clear drawbacks: if image conversion failed, there was no way to distinguish a failure in the representation itself from a failure in the write operation; if IPC was missing an argument, that could also obscure whether the completion timing for asynchronous opening was correct. This plan is no longer recommended for implementation, but it is retained because it explains why the early records did not list the callers separately.

Another earlier claim was that "the file depends directly on clipboard, so that file handles the image issue on its own." This is also corrected here: that dependency remains a useful starting point for investigation, but it is not enough to define the responsibility boundaries between object construction, caller input, and host writes. Expanding the image item to cover all clipboard behavior would also be inappropriate; this round covers only the segment where the image representation enters the write bridge.

## Retained Trial Approach for This Round

Behavior for the image item is now documented more clearly than in the first draft: The clipboard-writeImage bridge accepts a serialized representation, builds a nativeImage via createEmpty plus addRepresentation, and passes that image to clipboard.writeImage. The trial therefore no longer treats "writing the serialized representation directly" as a candidate path. Instead, it focuses on whether conversion from the representation to nativeImage should be placed inside the bridge. This does not extend to a unified model for clipboard read/write API.

For Shell.OpenExternal, the proposal retains only the goal of asynchronous completion; it does not invent a way for callers to wait. The review should start from an entry point still in use to confirm expectations after the call: if the caller relies only on initiating the operation, the bridge should not add new blocking semantics based on its name; if the caller depends on the completion result, then discuss how to return that result separately. Neither case can be settled by the conclusions for images.

Work on BrowserView IPC also stays narrow in scope. First obtain the argument order, optional argument positions, and argument-passing boundaries from an actual entry point, then determine where the existing route falls short of "with all arguments". Do not discard an argument early in the bridge layer just because it appears unused; do not write out an assumed fixed argument table without a sample.

At this point, the recommendation is to proceed in the following order, rather than submit a combined change:

- Images: trace from the host write boundary to the construction of nativeImage, keeping the serialized representation as the input;
- External open: find a caller entry point and distinguish the actual expectations for initiation versus completion;
- BrowserView: obtain a IPC call sample and check how every supplied argument maps to the route's receiving end.

These three steps share a review cadence, not rollback actions. If the image path forces existing callers to change their input, stop pursuing that path and propose a separate migration; if external open can only move forward by guessing at completion semantics, retain the existing call shape; if the sample for IPC does not yet establish the argument boundaries, do not mask the gap by filling in default values.

Still missing are an actual call sample for Shell.OpenExternal and the argument list for BrowserView IPC. The old proposal had no conclusion on either item; follow-up material should not generalize the object-construction process confirmed for the image bridge to those items.

Current decision for the existing clipboard-writeImage bridge: the caller passes a JSON string whose object maps each numeric scale factor to a base64 image byte string, together with the clipboard type. Decode every value before it is stored, and keep that representation's own scale factor with its decoded bytes; do not store or index the unparsed JSON text as the image. Each write replaces the previous image entirely. An empty byte string decodes to an empty buffer, and an empty object yields an image with no representations.

# Theme and Application State Migration Notes

The Bridge 12 review starts by grouping the old records into two sets: theme sources and contrast in one, and app focus and dock badge in the other. This grouping is only meant to recover the state fields left by callers; it does not mean all four share the same read/write mechanism.

The working assumption is that the theme-related records contain at least two kinds of things: values the native side could provide at the time, and choices the caller wanted to retain. Where old calls wrote them in the same place, migration cannot just rename fields; first establish whether the field is written before the call or read after it. Contrast must not be left next to the theme field merely as a note about the page color scheme, either.

Keep the original call order on the application side for now. The app focus options should stay near the call; record the dock badge display state separately. Early records described the two as "a single application update" because neither is part of the window content. That grouping helps when looking through old code, but it is not enough to establish whether the focus options were carried over.

The footer on the old troubleshooting page once pointed readers to `ElectronNET.WebApp/wwwroot/assets/highlight.min.js`. You can find `t(binding, line 3)` on the third line of the file, near a section of lexical rules for an existing js module:

```js
var t="[a-zA-Z_]\\w*[!?=]?|[-+~]\\@|<<|>>|=~|===?|<=>|[<>]=?|\\*\\*|[-/+%^&*~`|]|\\[\\]=?"
```

Retain this location as an old navigation reference for now. During migration, do not use these rules to infer where theme, contrast, app focus, or dock badge are implemented.

The tentative sequence is: first separate theme reads from theme selection; then keep contrast as an independent observation; next check that app focus calls still retain the original options; finally remove badge from the criteria for "focus call succeeded". # Theme and Application State Migration Record

The initial draft compressed four objects into two state records. The entry points can still be retained, but the merged representation will not be extended further. Theme source, contrast, app focus options, and the dock badge may all appear near the application layer, but the places where they are observed, written, or passed into calls are different. The goal of the migration is not to make the page appear to have only one state left, but to give the actions originally mixed together in legacy calls their own places again.

## Categories from the Initial Draft

The earliest diagram was meant to establish a rough direction in legacy calls:

```text
Theme source / contrast  ──> one theme record
app focus / badge ──> one application record
```

This diagram can still be used to identify legacy fields. If a field carries theme semantics, first check whether it also carries contrast; if an application-side record immediately follows a focus call, first check whether it also happens to write or read the badge. The diagram itself cannot be the post-migration data shape.

The initial draft's wording that "seeing a value after selecting is enough" also needs to be narrowed. A value may be the selection saved by the caller, or the state read at that time; if the two happen to be the same temporarily, legacy code will not expose the distinction. Renaming this kind of field directly to "current value" during migration would lock in the original ambiguity.

## Reviewing the Old Signposts

The review still starts at `ElectronNET.WebApp/wwwroot/assets/highlight.min.js`, listed in the old page footer. The file shows `t(binding, line 3)`; its third line is a lexical rule:

```js
var t="[a-zA-Z_]\\w*[!?=]?|[-+~]\\@|<<|>>|=~|===?|<=>|[<>]=?|\\*\\*|[-/+%^&*~`|]|\\[\\]=?"
```

Earlier, someone treated keywords near the path as the start of the state chain. This review found no such association. The file is an existing JS module. The lexical rule explains why the earlier reading started here, but not how the theme bridge or application calls are implemented.

Therefore, one note on the old page now reads: the path is only for recovering the reading position from that time. When you encounter it, stop at the declaration actually provided by the file; do not infer native behavior from neighboring words in the minified resource. The original judgment that "following this file would lead to the state entry point" remains in the old record; it is now deprecated.

## An Attempt at Splitting

While organizing, we tried writing theme selection, the read result, and page display as one continuous operation: write the selection first, read a value, and finally pass it to the page. The benefit was that it was easy to cross-check during debugging, but the migration record could not say what the read-back value represented. It might be only an echo of the selection, or the state from the current read; whether the page changes is a third matter.

At the time, folding contrast into the same explanation was also proposed. That approach was not carried forward. Contrast can sit next to the theme read, but it should not lose a separate observation point merely because the page's color result appears consistent.

The application side has the same problem. The old habit was to issue an app focus call, check whether the dock badge was still present, and then record "application state normal." This neither retained the options passed to focus nor said whether the badge was already present, was updated, or remained unchanged. Badge display cannot substitute for verifying the call input.

```text
Old record
  One theme field: selection / current value / contrast description
  One application record: focus call / badge display

after splitting
  Theme read       Theme selection      Contrast read
  focus options  badge state
```

These five positions are categories in the migration record, not a requirement for every caller to fill in all five. A call concerned only with the badge does not need to add a focus entry; a call that only reads contrast does not need to force in a theme selection.

## Review Addendum

The first counterexample raised in review was that the theme selection had already been written, but the page still had its original appearance. Looking only at the page would make it seem that the selection failed; looking only at the saved input would make it seem that the current state had changed. Neither conclusion can replace a separate read.

The second counterexample was that the page appearance changed, but no app focus call could be confirmed. Theme or contrast may also cause visible changes, so "the page looks correct" is not evidence that the focus options were passed.

There is also an old margin note that says "include the badge while updating focus." That sentence is retained as the troubleshooting sequence used at the time, not as a compatibility rule. During migration, the two actions can remain adjacent, but readers must be able to distinguish which part preserves the call options and which part handles the badge.

## Migration Landing Points

First mark the existing carriers in the legacy calls, rather than starting by replacing names with the new ones.

1. If a theme field is both written and read, mark the write and read actions separately; a field that cannot yet be split can continue serving legacy calls.
2. If contrast was previously embedded in the description of the theme field, leave a separate read location. If the caller does not care about it, do not invent a usage point.
3. Keep the original app focus options with the call. If migration leaves only result text such as "focused," the input has been lost.
4. Separate dock badge reads or updates from the focus-success check. The two pieces of code can be in the same method, but the record must no longer describe them as a single result.

Roll back per object. When the meaning of theme reads and writes is still unclear, stop adding new selection paths and retain the legacy field and the clues from the current read; when the contrast location is unclear, restore the caller-side's original display handling and do not put it back into theme selection; when focus options are unclear, restore the original parameter passing; when badge handling is unclear, restore only the badge path. An issue with the badge should not cause theme reads to revert to the old form as well.

## Combinations Not Yet Expanded

Some callers handle theme changes and dock display at the same time. The existing material only says that these two objects may occur in the same place; it does not establish that they share a state source. For calls like these, retain the combined action at this stage and state clearly what it read, submitted, and updated; do not rename it to the generic "application state synchronization".

# Theme and Application State Migration Record

This record gradually grew out of a small one-page checklist for Bridge 12. The initial goal was simply to recover what callers could see, but it later became clear that the old code and old notes had lumped different kinds of things together: theme source and contrast were called theme state, while app focus and dock badge were called application state. This classification was once useful, because it let people start from an ambiguous field and find their way back to the general area; it also led to many misinterpretations, because "state" did not say whether a value was read, selected, passed to a call, or displayed in the dock.

This page does not attempt to define an appearance policy for every caller. What is preserved here is the process of migrating from the old combined record to a verifiable record: which old statements should no longer be followed, which actions can be switched over one by one, and how to stay on the old path when the read/write direction is unclear. The historical sections have deliberately not been cleaned up into a guide that reads as though it were written in one pass, because when migrating old calls, the first things people actually encounter are often old fields, old signposts, and conclusions written in the margins.

---

## 2023-06-26: The Original Two Columns

The first draft used two columns, not interface layers.

```text
Theme source / contrast  ──> Theme record
app focus / badge ──> Application record
```

The goal at the time was simple: after seeing an old field, first decide which side to look under. Theme-related calls would usually leave a value that looked like the current setting; application-side calls would usually place a focus action and a badge display near each other. This gave rise to the two kinds of phrases "Theme synced" and "Application state normal" in the record.

Looking back now, both phrases were too broad. They did not distinguish whether the theme field actually held the caller's intent, a particular read, or the appearance ultimately used by the page; nor did they explain whether the app focus options still existed, or whether dock badge had been written to or simply happened to remain visible. The first draft is retained here because quite a few old calls were named after these two phrases. Simply deleting it would keep those handling later migrations from seeing where the conflation began.

The first draft also had a working assumption: after a theme was selected, if the caller could see a value, the action could be marked as complete. At the time, this assumption served only to find an entry point and did not account for cases where selection and reading might exist independently. In particular, it did not treat contrast separately. The subsequent review started with this gap.

An early margin note on the application side was even shorter: "Include badge when updating focus." It described the arrangement seen at the time, not an established relationship. If an old call happened to put a badge operation after a focus call, readers could easily interpret the order as a condition; the first draft did not leave enough material to rule out that interpretation.

## Static Assets in the Old Footer

Early footer troubleshooting brought some keywords to `ElectronNET.WebApp/wwwroot/assets/highlight.min.js`. The path has been retained because that is indeed where the earlier reading began. You can locate `t(binding, line 3)` on the third line of the file, with a block of lexical rules for an existing js module nearby:

```js
var t="[a-zA-Z_]\\w*[!?=]?|[-+~]\\@|<<|>>|=~|===?|<=>|[<>]=?|\\*\\*|[-/+%^&*~`|]|\\[\\]=?"
```

The old notes used words such as native, source, and state around this code. Someone used that as a basis for searching further through filenames and adjacent strings, trying to locate the bridge between theme and application state here. That line of investigation ultimately produced no usable conclusion: this declaration is a lexical rule and is not enough to establish ownership of theme source, contrast, app focus, or dock badge.

The path therefore has a very narrow current purpose: it is a signpost left by the old investigation notes. After opening the file, treat it only as a local declaration in an existing js module and a location examined in the past. Do not infer native calls from adjacent words in minified assets, and do not treat the file as the implementation entry point for the four migration items.

This is not meant to invalidate the old footer itself. The old footer can help explain why some investigation notes start with the static assets of WebApp; it cannot establish call relationships. The earlier sentence "Continue down from this file to see the state flow" has already been crossed out, and the old text remains here to prevent the next review from once again mistaking keyword matches for implementation ownership.

## 2023-09: Break down the terms first during review

The second pass did not start by changing the calling code, but instead began by breaking "state" in the old notes down into several kinds of actions. The same question about local use was asked of every old field: is it being read here, written here, or merely used by the caller for display? This seemingly simple question exposed differences that the initial draft's two columns could not express.

At least three distinct points emerged on the theme side: theme-related values read by the caller, the theme selection submitted by the caller, and the result the caller could see afterward. Contrast, meanwhile, was often found tucked away only in the explanatory text for theme fields. Writing it this way would make people mistake it for just a side effect of theme selection, rather than a state that needs separate attention.

Two points were also distinguished on the application side: the options carried by app focus calls, and the display state of dock badge. The two can continue to appear in the same method, even next to each other; the migration notes must identify which part is input and which part is display. Otherwise, as long as badge looks normal, the old notes will also judge focus propagation to be normal.

The shorthand recorded at the time was as follows:

```text
Read: the value obtained at the time
Selection: the mode submitted by the caller
Visible: the result the caller can still observe afterward
Input: the options carried by the app focus call
Display: the state of dock badge
```

These are not new public fields, nor are they a requirement for every caller to fill in all five items. They are only notations used during migration. A call concerned only with badge does not need to invent focus; a call that only reads contrast should not add a theme selection step just to keep the form consistent either. The purpose of breaking down the terms is to stop an old field from continuing to stand for things it does not actually describe.

## An attempt that did not preserve the distinctions

One earlier pass combined theme selection, theme reading, and page display into a continuous sequence: first write the selection, then retrieve a value, and finally pass that value to the page. Writing it that way kept the debugging steps short, and at first glance it also seemed easy to check the sequence in a single operation.

The problem is not that this sequence necessarily fails to run, but that the records lose their ability to answer questions later on. Does the value read back represent native's state at the time, or the selection the caller just saved? And is the change in the page's appearance caused by this value, contrast, or the caller's own styling logic? When the various outcomes temporarily match, the combined record reveals no problem; when they differ, the original notes no longer have anywhere to record the differences.

At one point, it was suggested that contrast be folded into the description of the "theme value", on the grounds that both affect appearance. This approach was later abandoned. A similar appearance is no reason to treat their read and write directions as the same. Contrast can sit alongside theme reads, but should not become a footnote to theme selection.

Similar omissions also appeared on the application side. Some old records observed the dock badge after an app focus call, and if the badge was still displayed, wrote "application state is normal". The record did not specify what options were passed to focus, nor whether the badge was already there, had just been updated, or had not changed at all. It merely turned two observations made close together into a single conclusion.

The diagram below preserves the structure of the records before and after this failed attempt. It shows how the migration notes separate observations, and does not require runtime execution to follow this top-to-bottom order:

```text
Before migration

  [Old theme-related fields]
       ├─ May be a read result
       ├─ May be the caller's selection
       └─ May be linked to a contrast description

  [Old application-related records]
       ├─ app focus call
       └─ dock badge display

After migration

  Theme read ────────────────┐
  Contrast read ──────────────┼─ Each gets its own place
  Theme selection ────────────────┘

  app focus options ──────── Kept separately
  dock badge state ─────── Observed separately
```

## Rejected old procedure section

The following passage comes from an earlier migration draft and retains its original line of thinking:

> First change the theme field, then observe the page; once the page changes, connect both app focus and badge to the same application update. If the page does not change, revert the entire block of changes.

This section no longer applies. First, it conflates the theme field's read and write directions into a single action; second, it treats a page change as shared proof for all objects; third, its rollback granularity is too coarse, so even a badge issue would roll back the theme path as well.

The old section has not been deleted because some callers happen to follow exactly this sequence. During migration, when you see code that "changes the field first, then checks the page, then includes badge", you do not need to first decide whether the page meets expectations. First, mark whether there is a theme read there, whether there is a theme selection, whether contrast is independent, where the focus options are, and whether badge is being read or updated. Some of these five items may be absent, but "the page changed" can no longer stand in for all of them.

Another old statement was "when focus takes effect, badge should update along with it". This has also been abandoned. It presented one observed sequence as a necessary relationship. The caller can maintain the badge state, and can also pass in the app focus options; the existing records provide no basis for treating the two as having the same source of state.

## Counterexamples in the review margins

What helped most during the review was not adding yet another overview table, but a few counterexamples that directly challenged the previous conclusions.

The first is: the theme selection has been written, but the page still shows the original color scheme. Looking only at the page would lead to the mistaken conclusion that the selection failed; looking only at the input saved by the caller would lead to the mistaken conclusion that the current state has changed. Neither view can replace a separate read. This overturns the initial draft's position that "a single value after selection is enough".

The second is: the page's appearance changes, but there is no verifiable app focus call. Either theme or contrast could cause a change in appearance, and the caller may also apply its own styling. Therefore, a page that looks normal does not prove that the app focus options are still being passed along the original path.

The third is: dock badge remains unchanged. Earlier records tended to interpret this as focus having no effect; in fact, it only shows that the badge display does not provide enough information. It proves neither that the focus input was retained nor that the input was lost.

The brief statement left after the review was: theme entries must at least distinguish the current-state read from the selection action; application entries must at least distinguish the focus input from the badge display. This statement only governs how this migration record is written. It does not prescribe a uniform color scheme strategy for caller pages, nor does it define visual outcomes on all platforms as one and the same thing.

## Migration starts with the legacy representation

In practice, migration does not require replacing all legacy calls at once. First, document the existing representation at each call site, then decide whether to split it. The representation may be a field, an argument position in a call, a read, or simply a piece of display handling. When things are unclear, retaining the original name and order is safer than giving it a polished new name.

**When there is only one theme field.**

First, check where it is written and where it is read. If writes express a selection while reads express the current state, do not continue making the same field carry both meanings. The old field can remain temporarily for consumers that have not yet migrated; for the new path, start keeping records at two locations. If contrast is mentioned only in the description, first move it to a separate observation point rather than expanding the old field's comment.

**When theme and contrast are already separate.**

There is no need to merge them again just to standardize the format. The migration only needs to preserve each item's read location and prevent theme selection from overriding the meaning of contrast. If the caller only cares about one of them, keep that limited scope; this page does not require adding a call for the other item just for completeness.

**When app focus and dock badge are in the same method.**

First, make sure the options passed to app focus remain visible. Then document the badge read or update as a separate record. The method does not have to be forcibly split just because the documentation is split, but subsequent readers should be able to identify which part is call input and which part is display state. Do not use the badge result to backfill the focus options.

**When the caller only handles dock badge.**

Record only badge. If there is no app focus call, there are no focus options to migrate. Inventing a relationship just to make the page structure tidy is exactly how the early two-column records caused confusion.

**When badge is also handled during a theme change.**

This is a combined action by the caller and does not automatically mean that the two share common bridge semantics. First retain the theme-related actions and badge handling separately, then confirm why the caller put them together. When the reason is unclear, preserve the combination and the open question rather than rewriting it as a unified state source.

## Local rollback

Restore legacy paths on a per-object basis as well, rather than rolling back the entire block. The approaches below preserve usable entry points for legacy adopters, not re-endorse the semantics of legacy fields.

| Area of uncertainty | What is temporarily retained | How to restore |
| --- | --- | --- |
| The meaning of the value read after theme selection is unclear | Clues from the current read and the legacy field | Stop extending the selection path, restore the legacy field to where it was originally used |
| Contrast still has no place of its own | Theme reads | Restore the caller's original display handling, do not squeeze contrast into the selection field |
| The app focus options are unclear after the adjustment | Original call arguments | Restore the original argument passing, do not use badge display as a proxy for the decision |
| The dock badge state is unclear | Original badge handling | Restore the badge path separately, without rolling back theme reads or selection |

"Restoring the legacy field" does not mean calling it the current state again. During rollback, retain the distinctions already identified this time: which write is a selection, which read is treated as the current value, where contrast was originally hidden, and whether badge was used as a substitute for determining focus. Otherwise, the next migration round will start over at the same point of conflation.

## 2025-07-21: Current theme interface contract

The preceding two columns, misinterpretation of static assets, supplementary term-breakdown notes, attempts at merging, and review counterexamples all demonstrate one thing: theme-related calls can no longer be closed out with "the theme is synchronized". The current migration requirements are as follows:

`nativeTheme-shouldUseHighContrastColors returns Electron's current value, while nativeTheme-themeSource accepts a supported ThemeSourceMode and leaves the selected mode observable.`

This statement is included only here and is not written back into earlier records. High contrast corresponds to the current read; the theme source accepts supported modes; the selected mode must still be observable by the caller. When a legacy call has only one field, that field can continue serving the unmigrated parts for now, but new reads and new selections must no longer be conflated through it.

This theme interface contract does not replace app focus or dock badge. Migrating them still requires examining two local objects: the options actually retained by the focus call, and the display state of badge itself. Putting all four items in the same record is intended to address traces of conflation in legacy calls, not to declare that they share the semantics of the theme interface.

## Questions remaining on this page

Some callers care about both theme changes and dock display, making it easy to once again propose "a unified badge refresh after a theme change". For now, this is not being written as a rule. The existing material can only show that the two often appear in the same caller, not that they share a state source or have a fixed order.

Going forward, if you encounter calls like these, first record four specific things: whether the theme or contrast is read, whether a theme selection is submitted, whether app focus is called with options, and whether badge is read or updated. Until these actions have been separated, do not add a catch-all application state field, and do not use the page's final appearance as a substitute for any of them.

## Archived legacy examples

**Legacy example A: One field handles everything about the theme.**

The legacy call stored the theme source, contrast, and page display semantics in the same field. This example is outdated, but it can still help identify code that needs to be split up. The first step in migration is not to rename the field, but to identify separately when it is written, when it is read, and whether contrast appears only in comments.

**Legacy example B: Using badge to determine whether focus succeeded.**

The legacy call checked dock badge after app focus and recorded badge visibility as focus success. This judgment was later rejected. The visibility of badge cannot serve as evidence of the focus options. When you encounter this pattern, the existing badge handling can be retained, but the focus options must be moved back to a separate verification step.

**Legacy example C: Tracing state implementation from static assets.**

The old footer pointed to `ElectronNET.WebApp/wwwroot/assets/highlight.min.js`, after which someone treated the lexical rules on the third line as the start of the state flow. This reading approach has since been corrected: the file is useful only as a historical reference point. It provides no conclusions about the implementation of theme, contrast, focus, or badge.

Legacy examples are not a substitute for the current migration steps. They document why legacy calls ended up with combined fields, adjacent operations, and misleading signposts. When you encounter these traces, record each object separately, then migrate each item to the new observation approach.

# Bridge 12 Host Boundary Troubleshooting

This troubleshooting page remains in the old on-call entry for Bridge 12. The entry originally received two very short reports: generated hosts had no dock assets, or Linux host builds did not produce the expected result. Both contained the word host, so the initial draft compressed them into one Host API issue and fixed the first step as opening `ElectronNET.Host/api/clipboard.ts`.

The old draft was not deleted because later questions still follow that path. Some people only remember that they "looked at the Host side," while others only remember the filename and do not know that the two types of reports were treated as one omission at the time. What follows preserves the sequence from then; it is not a repair plan to follow directly.

> **Old conclusion, later overturned.** `clipboard.ts` imports Electron's `clipboard`, so generated-host assets and Linux Host builds very likely share one piece of Host wiring; change here first, then inspect the generated result.

The file header does indeed contain this line:

```ts
import { clipboard } from 'electron';
```

This import line can confirm only a very narrow scope: the file is directly adjacent to the Electron clipboard API. It cannot prove that dock assets enter the generated host from here; nor can it prove that Linux builds start here. The problem with the old conclusion was not that the file did not exist, but that it turned "being able to navigate to a Host API file" into "the two phenomena have the same implementation ownership."

The old records also contain a shortcut: when a report mentioned generated host, Linux, and API at the same time, they were assigned to the same change point. This makes the asset issue borrow the build issue's context, and the build issue borrow the asset issue's description. The missing material on the two sides is different, so they cannot replace each other.

---

## Branch by Report First

When handling a report, do not first ask which file should be modified. First check what type of material the report actually provides. The tree below retains the old entry and the stopping points added later; each "Stop" means that the description cannot yet be advanced into an implementation conclusion.

```text
Bridge 12 report
|
+-- Ship dock assets in generated hosts
|   |
|   +-- Can obtain the generated-host directory
|   |   |
|   |   +-- The resource indicated by the report is in the directory
|   |   |   `-- No longer treat it as "not included during generation"; trace back the location indicated by the report
|   |   |
|   |   `-- The resource indicated by the report is not in the directory
|   |       `-- Record the directory observation; continue checking the generated-host asset boundary
|   |
|   `-- Only a description of "missing dock assets"
|       `-- Stop: do not fill in the asset name, default directory, or platform conditions
|
`-- Run Linux host builds from ElectronNET.Host
    |
    +-- There is an actual CI run
    |   |
    |   +-- The run record shows that ElectronNET.Host was executed
    |   |   `-- Then check the result of that run
    |   |
    |   `-- It is unclear whether Host was executed
    |       `-- Record it as an unconfirmed build entry point
    |
    `-- There is no actual CI run
        `-- Stop: the existence of configuration files and paths does not mean the build took effect
```

The first branch of the tree handles only the asset boundary within generated hosts. If the report can provide a directory after generation, it becomes possible to distinguish between "the resource is already inside the generated host" and "the resource did not enter the generated host." The former can no longer be called a loading gap; the latter is only enough to keep the issue at the generated-host asset boundary. Directory observation still cannot establish that a specific copy rule, project configuration, or API file is the cause.

ENB-212 is the navigation card for this branch. It requires reusing the command key phrase "Ship dock assets in generated hosts" from the report issue, without filling in hidden environments or default files on the report's behalf. The most common drift in the old on-call records was to replace dock assets directly with some assumed asset name and then search for a file based on that assumption; the resulting answer could not be traced back to the original report. Putting the card into a processing state only means that this boundary has been captured; it does not mean that directory material is available or that the asset issue has been located.

The reason the initial draft first looked at clipboard.ts is preserved here as well: at the time, "generated host" was understood as the visible manifestation of Host API wiring. This understanding led people to trace calls outward from the import. The file can still be opened to confirm whether you are in the area adjacent to Host API; but when review finds only this import, the record should stop at "confirmed clipboard adjacency," and must not be written as "confirmed asset loading path."

---

## The Old Misreading of the Linux Branch

The other branch concerns "Run Linux host builds from ElectronNET.Host." The old draft conflated the existence of a Host file, the project being openable, and the build actually running. As a result, some people saw the `ElectronNET.Host` directory and recorded the Linux branch as already executed; others did not see the expected output and inferred that the Host API wiring was missing. Neither inference was based on an actual CI run.

The Linux branch must have a run record first. Once the record is available, the first thing to check is whether it can confirm that the run executed `ElectronNET.Host`. If the record cannot distinguish this, the build entry point remains unconfirmed; do not fill in the execution process from the project configuration, filename, or import. Only after confirming that Host was executed should you continue to check whether that run itself supports the next troubleshooting step.

ENB-217 is used to return to this entry. The card once contained a handoff confirmation, so the old version misread "handed off" as confirmation that the Linux path was already confirmed. The correction here is: a handoff confirmation only indicates that the investigation was transferred; it cannot replace a CI run. The card description requires confirming in a real CI run whether "Run Linux host builds from ElectronNET.Host" took effect; the existence of a configuration file must not be used in place of the run result.

This branch does not require reading clipboard.ts first. If the run record already shows that the build entry point is unclear, returning to the API file will only disguise the unclear state as a code clue; if the run record is sufficient to confirm that Host was executed, whether API adjacency needs to be checked depends on the subsequent clues provided by that run, not on the old manual's default order.

---

## The Procedure Order Still Retained

The old page originally listed three steps:

1. Open `ElectronNET.Host/api/clipboard.ts`.
2. After finding the clipboard import, assume that the assets and Linux builds share Host wiring.
3. When no gap is apparent, wait for generated-host material.

The 1 step is now suitable only for explaining the entry point of the old report or performing a very narrow API adjacency check. The 2 step is no longer applicable and cannot be a premise for any modification. The 3 step is retained, but must be understood separately: the asset branch waits for a generated-host directory; the Linux branch waits for an actual CI run. They are both called "supplying material," but they are not the same kind of material.

This is also why the page can still easily mislead people. The title puts the two subjects together, and the old draft provided a shared Host starting point, so readers can easily assume that one review can close both branches at once. In reality, the branches must be separated first, and then each branch must be assessed for whether it has the conditions to continue troubleshooting. Even if both pieces of material appear, that does not automatically indicate that they point to the same file or the same regression.

## Note Beside the Old Entry

For an asset report, first confirm whether a generated-host directory is available; if there is no directory, retain the scope of the original report and do not fill in a filename for it. For a Linux report, first confirm whether there is an actual CI run; if there is no run, do not record the existence of the configuration as meaning that the build took effect. Only when these two minimum conditions are met separately should you continue discussing the next step for each branch.

DOC-20 records another migration track for tray and notification registry. The old on-call entry once placed it beside the Host-related material, but it does not provide a basis for assessing dock assets or Linux builds, so do not borrow conclusions from it here.

This page retains clipboard.ts, the two old objects, and traces of the originally merged branch so that readers can understand why the old reports entered the same entry. It is not a final statement about generated-host assets or Linux build status.

# Tray and notification registry migration checks

At the start of the Bridge 12 checks, tray and notification registration were covered by the same compatibility check. The initial concern wasn't whether the UI appeared, but whether the objects could still be found through the same object relationships on re-entry after a host lifecycle ended. The notes at the time listed `ElectronNET.WebApp/wwwroot/assets/highlight.min.js` as the starting point for investigation; that location came from the old checklist and doesn't mean the registration logic is in that file.

The old approach was to keep temporary records of the tray and notification objects seen on each startup, then refer back to them for the current instance. That was enough for a single debugging session, but the records would get mixed together when a window was reopened, the host was re-entered, or events arrived late. During migration, don't yet combine the two object types into a single "restored" conclusion: if there is a result for tray but none for notification, keep that as an incomplete migration state.

Follow this order:

1. First, copy the tray and notification names, the actions that created them, and whether they depended on a particular host state at the time from the old checklist. If a name is uncertain, leave it blank; don't fill it in with a similar window or module name.
2. Run continuity checks for the tray registry and notification registry separately. As each check is completed, record its lookup results before and after reopening; don't overwrite results already obtained because the other check is still under investigation.
3. For items that need to persist across lifecycles, add a lookup record after re-entry. The check here is whether the registry can still be located, not recreating a tray item or notification that looks the same.
4. Replace the "visible on this startup" flags in the old table with two possible results: confirmed to have remained present, or visible only on this startup. Keep the latter on the old path; don't mark them as successfully migrated yet.

There was an unverified assumption at the time: as long as the host state remained, both registries would be retained together, so the process-global registry was not recorded separately. This assumption is retained here because the old investigation checklist used it as the basis for skipping the repeat lookup of notification; the migration must not carry over that omission.

When restoring the old path, remove the continuity conclusions added in this round and restore the table entries that keep records separate for each startup. Don't delete objects that were observed but haven't yet been located again; just reset their status to "visible on this startup". That way, the next round can continue from the original names and actions without making unconfirmed items look persisted.

Two points are still unresolved: which objects in the old records actually survived a host lifecycle, and whether tray and notification share the same registration entry point. Until these are resolved, the Bridge 12 check results can only be recorded at the object level; they cannot state that the entire group of registries has been migrated.
